1.6 Encode Categoricals & Scale Numerics¶

In [10]:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X = df.drop("income", axis=1)
y = df["income"]

# One-Hot Encode Categorical Columns
X = pd.get_dummies(X, drop_first=True)

print("Shape after One-Hot Encoding:", X.shape)

num_cols = [
    "age",
    "educational-num",
    "capital-gain",
    "capital-loss",
    "hours-per-week"
]

scaler = StandardScaler()
X[num_cols] = scaler.fit_transform(X[num_cols])

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X,
    y,
    test_size=0.20,
    random_state=42,
    stratify=y
)

print("\nTraining Features :", X_train.shape)
print("Testing Features  :", X_test.shape)
print("Training Labels   :", y_train.shape)
print("Testing Labels    :", y_test.shape)

print("\nTraining Class Distribution")
print(y_train.value_counts(normalize=True))

print("\nTesting Class Distribution")
print(y_test.value_counts(normalize=True))

Task 2: MLP Architecture — Baseline ANN¶

2.1 Define the Reusable build_ann() Function¶

In [11]:
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras.models import Sequential
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Dense, BatchNormalization

def build_ann(
    input_dim,
    hidden_units=[128, 64],
    activation="relu",
    initializer="glorot_uniform",
    use_batch_norm=False,
    optimizer="adam",
    loss="binary_crossentropy"
):
    model = Sequential()

    # First Hidden Layer
    model.add(Dense(hidden_units[0],
                    activation=activation,
                    kernel_initializer=initializer,
                    input_dim=input_dim))

    if use_batch_norm:
        model.add(BatchNormalization())

    # Second Hidden Layer
    model.add(Dense(hidden_units[1],
                    activation=activation,
                    kernel_initializer=initializer))

    if use_batch_norm:
        model.add(BatchNormalization())

    # Output Layer
    model.add(Dense(1, activation="sigmoid"))

    # Compile Model
    model.compile(
        optimizer=optimizer,
        loss=loss,
        metrics=["accuracy"]
    )

    return model
  • A reusable build_ann() function was created to build different ANN models easily.
  • The function allows changing parameters such as hidden units, activation function, optimizer, initializer, and batch normalization.
  • Using a single function ensures all future experiments are consistent and only one parameter changes at a time.

  • The baseline ANN consists of two hidden layers with 128 and 64 neurons using the ReLU activation function.
  • The output layer contains one neuron with a Sigmoid activation function because this is a binary classification problem.
  • Sigmoid produces an output between 0 and 1, representing the probability of belonging to the positive class (>50K income).

Why Sigmoid is Used?¶

  • Sigmoid is used because the problem has only two classes (<=50K and >50K).
  • It returns a probability value between 0 and 1.
  • A single output neuron with Sigmoid is more efficient than using two output neurons with Softmax for binary classification.
In [13]:
from tensorflow import keras
from tensorflow.keras import layers

# Build Baseline ANN
model_base = keras.Sequential([

    layers.Dense(
        128,
        activation="relu",
        kernel_initializer="glorot_uniform",
        input_shape=(X_train.shape[1],)
    ),

    layers.Dense(
        64,
        activation="relu",
        kernel_initializer="glorot_uniform"
    ),

    layers.Dense(
        1,
        activation="sigmoid"
    )

])

# Compile Model
model_base.compile(
    optimizer="adam",
    loss="binary_crossentropy",
    metrics=["accuracy"]
)

# Display Model Summary
model_base.summary()

Why Sigmoid is Used Instead of Softmax?¶

The Adult Income dataset is a binary classification problem with two classes: <=50K and >50K.

  • Sigmoid produces a single probability between 0 and 1, representing the probability that a sample belongs to the positive class (>50K).
  • If the probability is greater than 0.5, the sample is classified as class 1; otherwise, it is classified as class 0.
  • A single Sigmoid output neuron is more efficient than using a two-neuron Softmax layer for binary classification because it requires fewer parameters while providing the same decision capability.

Therefore, Sigmoid is the preferred activation function for the output layer in binary classification tasks.

2.4 Evaluate the Baseline with Full Metrics¶

from sklearn.metrics import (
    classification_report,
    confusion_matrix,
    ConfusionMatrixDisplay
)

# Predict Probabilities
y_pred_prob = model_base.predict(X_test).flatten()

# Convert Probabilities into Classes
y_pred = (y_pred_prob > 0.5).astype(int)

# Classification Report
print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred))

  • Precision, Recall, and F1-score for the >50K class are important because it is the minority class.

2.5 Why Tabular Data Suits ANN¶

Structured tabular data is well suited for an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) because each input feature (such as age, education, work hours, and capital gain) can be directly connected to an input neuron. Unlike images or sequential data, tabular datasets do not require specialized architectures like CNNs or RNNs.

The hidden layers of an ANN learn complex relationships between features by combining weighted inputs and applying non-linear activation functions. This enables the model to capture patterns such as the interaction between age and education or working hours and occupation, which are difficult for simpler models like Logistic Regression to learn.

Therefore, a fully connected Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) is a suitable choice for binary classification problems on structured tabular datasets such as the Adult Income dataset.

Task 3: Activation Functions — Comparison Experiment¶

3.1 Train 4 Models with Different Hidden Activations¶

In [21]:
# ReLU Model
model_relu = build_ann(input_dim=X_train.shape[1], activation="relu")
history_relu = model_relu.fit(
    X_train, y_train,
    epochs=50,
    batch_size=64,
    validation_split=0.1,
    verbose=1
)

# Tanh Model
model_tanh = build_ann(input_dim=X_train.shape[1], activation="tanh")
history_tanh = model_tanh.fit(
    X_train, y_train,
    epochs=50,
    batch_size=64,
    validation_split=0.1,
    verbose=1
)

# Sigmoid Model
model_sigmoid = build_ann(input_dim=X_train.shape[1], activation="sigmoid")
history_sigmoid = model_sigmoid.fit(
    X_train, y_train,
    epochs=50,
    batch_size=64,
    validation_split=0.1,
    verbose=1
)

# ELU Model
model_elu = build_ann(input_dim=X_train.shape[1], activation="elu")
history_elu = model_elu.fit(
    X_train, y_train,
    epochs=50,

)

3.2 Activation Comparison – 4-Panel Plot¶

In [68]:
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score

histories = {
    "ReLU": (history_relu, model_relu),
    "Tanh": (history_tanh, model_tanh),
    "Sigmoid": (history_sigmoid, model_sigmoid),
    "ELU": (history_elu, model_elu)
}

plt.figure(figsize=(14,10))

for i, (name, (history, model)) in enumerate(histories.items(), start=1):

    y_pred = (model.predict(X_test).flatten() > 0.5).astype(int)

    f1 = f1_score(y_test, y_pred)
    val_acc = history.history["val_accuracy"][-1]

    plt.subplot(2,2,i)

    # Training Accuracy
    plt.plot(
        history.history["accuracy"],
        color="#66C2A5",
        linewidth=2,
        label="Training Accuracy"

    # Validation Accuracy
    plt.plot(
        history.history["val_accuracy"],
        color="#FC8D62",
        linewidth=2,
        label="Validation Accuracy"
    )

    # Baseline
    plt.axhline(
        y=0.75,
        linestyle="--",
        color="gray",
        label="75% Baseline"
    )

    plt.title(f"{name}\nVal Acc={val_acc:.3f} | F1={f1:.3f}")
    plt.xlabel("Epoch")
    plt.ylabel("Accuracy")
    plt.grid(alpha=0.3)
    plt.legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

3.3 Dead Neuron Check – ReLU¶

In [23]:
from tensorflow.keras.models import Model

# Ensure the model is built explicitly if its input property is not readily available
model_relu.build(input_shape=(None, X_train.shape[1]))

intermediate = Model(
    inputs=model_relu.layers[0].input, # Changed to access input via the first layer
    outputs=model_relu.layers[0].output
)

activations = intermediate.predict(X_test[:500], verbose=0)

dead_fraction = np.mean(activations == 0)

print(f"Dead Fraction: {dead_fraction:.4f}")

mean_activation = activations.mean(axis=0)

# Plot Histogram
plt.figure(figsize=(8,5))
plt.hist(mean_activation, bins=20, edgecolor="black", color="skyblue")
plt.title("ReLU First-Layer Activation Distribution")
plt.xlabel("Mean Activation per Neuron")
plt.ylabel("Number of Neurons")
plt.show()

Dead Fraction: 0.6196
  • The activations of the first hidden layer were extracted for 500 test samples.
  • The dead fraction measures the percentage of ReLU outputs that are exactly 0.

Why ELU Avoids Dead Neurons¶

ReLU outputs 0 for all negative input values. If a neuron keeps producing zero, it stops updating its weights because its gradient becomes zero. This problem is called the Dead Neuron Problem.

The ELU (Exponential Linear Unit) activation function reduces this problem by producing small negative outputs for negative inputs instead of zero:

[ ELU(x)= \begin{cases} x, & x>0 \\ \alpha(e^x-1), & x\le0 \end{cases} ]

Because ELU provides a non-zero gradient for negative inputs, neurons continue to learn during training. This keeps the gradient flowing and reduces the number of dead neurons, often leading to better convergence than ReLU.

3.4 Gradient Flow Check – Sigmoid Hidden Layers¶

In [24]:
X_batch = tf.convert_to_tensor(X_train[:64], dtype=tf.float32)
y_batch = tf.convert_to_tensor(y_train[:64].values.reshape(-1, 1), dtype=tf.float32)

with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
    predictions = model_sigmoid(X_batch, training=True)
    loss = tf.keras.losses.binary_crossentropy(y_batch, predictions)
    loss = tf.reduce_mean(loss)

gradients = tape.gradient(loss, model_sigmoid.trainable_weights)

layer_names = []
gradient_values = []

# Create a list of (weight_variable, gradient_tensor) pairs for easy lookup
weight_grad_pairs = list(zip(model_sigmoid.trainable_weights, gradients))

for layer in model_sigmoid.layers:
    if isinstance(layer, tf.keras.layers.Dense):
        kernel_weights_var = layer.kernel # This is the tf.Variable for the kernel

        # Find the gradient corresponding to this kernel_weights_var by object identity
        grad_for_kernel = None
        for weight_var, grad_val in weight_grad_pairs:
            if weight_var is kernel_weights_var: # Compare by object identity
                grad_for_kernel = grad_val
                break

        if grad_for_kernel is not None:
            layer_names.append(layer.name)
            gradient_values.append(tf.reduce_mean(tf.abs(grad_for_kernel)).numpy())
        else:
            # Handle cases where a kernel might not have a gradient (e.g., if it's not trainable)
            layer_names.append(layer.name)
            gradient_values.append(0.0) # Assign 0 or NaN if no gradient was found

plt.figure(figsize=(8,4))
plt.barh(layer_names, gradient_values)
plt.xlabel("Mean |Gradient|")
plt.ylabel("Dense Layer")
plt.title("Gradient Magnitude by Layer — Sigmoid Hidden Activations")
plt.show()

for name, value in zip(layer_names, gradient_values):
    print(f"{name}: {value:.6f}")

dense_15: 0.000206
dense_16: 0.000244
dense_17: 0.005600
  • The gradient magnitude was computed for each Dense layer using TensorFlow's GradientTape.
  • If the first hidden layer has much smaller gradients than the output layer, it indicates the vanishing gradient problem.

Why Vanishing Gradient Occurs¶

The maximum value of this derivative is 0.25. During backpropagation, gradients are multiplied across layers. Since these values are always less than or equal to 0.25, the gradient becomes smaller after passing through each hidden layer.

As a result, the early layers receive extremely small weight updates, making training slow and less effective. This phenomenon is known as the Vanishing Gradient Problem.

3.5 Activation Summary Table¶

Activation Function Comparison¶

Activation Formula Output Range Zero-Centred Vanishing Gradient Risk Dead Neuron Risk Validation Accuracy
ReLU max(0, x) [0, ∞) No Low Yes Enter your result
Tanh tanh(x) (-1, 1) Yes Medium No Enter your result
Sigmoid 1 / (1 + e⁻ˣ) (0, 1) No High No Enter your result
ELU x (x>0), α(eˣ−1) (x≤0) (-α, ∞) Nearly Low Very Low Enter your result

Recommendation¶

  • ReLU is generally the best choice because it trains faster and performs well on tabular datasets.
  • ELU is also an excellent choice as it reduces the dead neuron problem while maintaining good performance.
  • Tanh performs reasonably well but may train more slowly than ReLU.
  • Sigmoid is not recommended for hidden layers because it is prone to the vanishing gradient problem.

Note: The Sigmoid activation in the output layer is always the correct choice for binary classification, regardless of the hidden layer activation function.

Task 4: Weight Initialization Techniques¶

4.1 Train 5 Models with Different Initialisers¶

In [25]:
# Glorot Uniform
model_glorot_uniform = build_ann(
    input_dim=X_train.shape[1],
    activation="relu",
    initializer="glorot_uniform"
)

history_glorot_uniform = model_glorot_uniform.fit(
    X_train,

  • Five ANN models were trained using different weight initialization techniques.
  • All other hyperparameters were kept the same to ensure a fair comparison.
  • The effect of each initialization method on model convergence and performance can now be analyzed.
  • The Zeros initializer is included only for comparison because it usually performs poorly due to the symmetry problem.

4.2 Why Initialisation Matters¶

Weight initialization plays an important role in training a neural network. If all weights are initialized to zero, every neuron in the same layer produces the same output, receives the same gradient, and updates in exactly the same way. This is called the symmetry problem, and it prevents the network from learning different features.

Xavier (Glorot) Initialization is designed for activation functions such as Sigmoid and Tanh. It keeps the variance of activations and gradients stable across layers, helping the network learn efficiently.

He Initialization is specially designed for ReLU activation. Since ReLU sets negative values to zero, about half of the neurons become inactive during each forward pass. He initialization compensates for this by using a larger variance, which helps maintain stable activations and improves convergence.

Therefore, choosing the correct initialization method improves learning speed, training stability, and overall model performance.

colors = ["blue", "green", "red", "purple", "black"]
linestyles = ["-", "--", "-.", ":", "-"]

for (name, history), color, style in zip(histories.items(), colors, linestyles):

    val_acc = history.history["val_accuracy"]

    plt.plot(
        val_acc,
        label=name,
        color=color,
        linestyle=style,
        linewidth=2
    )

    # First epoch crossing 82%
    for epoch, acc in enumerate(val_acc):
        if acc >= 0.82:
            plt.axvline(
                x=epoch,
                color=color,
                linestyle=":",
                alpha=0.6
            )
            break

# Target Benchmark
plt.axhline(
    y=0.84,
    color="gray",
    linestyle="--",
    label="84% Target"
)

plt.title("Weight Initialization — Convergence Speed Comparison")
plt.xlabel("Epoch")
plt.ylabel("Validation Accuracy")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()
  • The validation accuracy of all five initialization methods was compared.
  • Vertical lines indicate the first epoch where a model reached 82% validation accuracy.

Task 5: Loss Functions¶

5.1 Binary Cross-Entropy – The Correct Loss Function¶

In [31]:
# Confirm the loss function used in the baseline model
print("Baseline Loss Function:", model_base.loss)

Baseline Loss Function: binary_crossentropy

Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE)¶

The baseline ANN model uses Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) because this is a binary classification problem.

The Binary Cross-Entropy loss is:

$$ L = -\left( y \log(p) + (1-y)\log(1-p) \right) $$

Where:

  • y = True label (0 or 1)
  • p = Predicted probability from the Sigmoid output layer

BCE strongly penalizes confident incorrect predictions.

For example:

  • If y = 1 but p = 0, then log(0) → -∞, producing a very large loss.
  • If y = 0 but p = 1, the loss is also very large.

Therefore, Binary Cross-Entropy is the natural choice for binary classification because it measures how well the predicted probabilities match the true labels.

Why MSE is Not Suitable for Classification¶

Mean Squared Error (MSE) treats the output of the Sigmoid neuron as a regression value instead of a probability for classification.

Unlike Binary Cross-Entropy, MSE does not strongly penalize confident incorrect predictions. Its gradients also become very small when the Sigmoid output is close to 0 or 1, slowing the learning process.

Binary Cross-Entropy has better gradient behavior for binary classification, allowing the network to learn faster and achieve better performance, especially on imbalanced datasets like the Adult Income dataset.

Therefore, Binary Cross-Entropy is the preferred loss function for binary classification, while MSE is better suited for regression problems.

5.3 Weighted Binary Cross-Entropy – Handling Class Imbalance¶

In [35]:
from sklearn.utils.class_weight import compute_class_weight

# Compute Class Weights
classes = np.unique(y_train)

weights = compute_class_weight(
    class_weight="balanced",
    classes=classes,
    y=y_train
)

# Create Class Weight Dictionary
class_weight = {
    0: weights[0],
    1: weights[1]
}

print("Class Weights:")
print(class_weight)

Why Weighted Binary Cross-Entropy?¶

The Adult Income dataset is imbalanced because the number of <=50K samples is much larger than the number of >50K samples.

Weighted Binary Cross-Entropy assigns a higher loss weight to the minority class (>50K). This means that mistakes on minority-class samples are penalized more heavily during training.

As a result:

  • The model pays more attention to the minority class.
  • Recall for the >50K class usually improves.
  • F1-score often improves because more positive samples are correctly identified.
  • Precision may decrease slightly because the model predicts more positive cases.

Weighted BCE is useful when missing a high-income individual is more costly than predicting a false positive, making it suitable for imbalanced binary classification problems.

5.4 Focal Loss – Advanced Imbalance Handling¶

In [39]:
def focal_loss(gamma=2.0, alpha=0.25):

    def loss(y_true, y_pred):

        y_pred = tf.clip_by_value(y_pred, 1e-7, 1 - 1e-7)

        bce = -(
            y_true * tf.math.log(y_pred) +
            (1 - y_true) * tf.math.log(1 - y_pred)
        )

        weight = (
            alpha * y_true * tf.pow(1 - y_pred, gamma) +
            (1 - alpha) * (1 - y_true) * tf.pow(y_pred, gamma)
        )

        return tf.reduce_mean(weight * bce)

    return loss

Why Focal Loss?¶

Focal Loss was introduced by Facebook AI (Lin et al., 2017) to improve learning on highly imbalanced datasets.

Unlike Binary Cross-Entropy, Focal Loss reduces the contribution of easy-to-classify samples and focuses more on hard, misclassified samples.

The term (1 − p)^γ reduces the loss for correctly classified examples while increasing the importance of difficult examples. This allows the model to pay more attention to the minority class and often improves Recall and F1-score on imbalanced datasets.

5.5 Loss Function Summary Table¶

Loss Function Comparison¶

Loss Function Formula (Simplified) Best For Imbalance Handling Class-1 F1 Score
Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) -[ylog(p)+(1-y)log(1-p)] Binary Classification Good Enter your result
Weighted BCE Weighted BCE Imbalanced Classification Very Good Enter your result
Mean Squared Error (MSE) (y-p)² Regression Poor Enter your result
Focal Loss (1-p)^γ × BCE Highly Imbalanced Data Excellent Enter your result

Recommendation¶

  • Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) is the standard loss function for binary classification.
  • Weighted BCE is recommended when the dataset is imbalanced because it gives more importance to the minority class.
  • Focal Loss is the best choice for highly imbalanced datasets as it focuses training on hard-to-classify samples.
  • Mean Squared Error (MSE) is not suitable for classification because it treats the problem like regression.

Recommended Loss Function: Weighted BCE (or Focal Loss if it achieves a higher F1-score on your results), as both are well suited for the Adult Income dataset with class imbalance.

from tensorflow import keras
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Dense, BatchNormalization, Activation

# Build ANN with Batch Normalization
model_bn = keras.Sequential([

    Dense(
        128,
        kernel_initializer="he_normal",
        input_shape=(X_train.shape[1],)
    ),

    BatchNormalization(),
    Activation("relu"),

    Dense(
        64,
        kernel_initializer="he_normal"
    ),

    BatchNormalization(),
    Activation("relu"),

    Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")

])

# Compile Model
model_bn.compile(
    optimizer="adam",
    loss="binary_crossentropy",
    metrics=["accuracy"]
)

# Display Model Summary
model_bn.summary()

6.2 Why Batch Normalization Matters¶

Why Batch Normalization?¶

During training, the weights of each layer are continuously updated. As a result, the distribution of inputs to the next layer also changes. This is known as Internal Covariate Shift, which makes training slower and more difficult.

Batch Normalization solves this by normalizing the inputs of each mini-batch to have approximately zero mean and unit variance. After normalization, it applies two learnable parameters:

  • γ (Gamma): Learns the optimal scale.
  • β (Beta): Learns the optimal shift.

The Batch Normalization equation is:

$$ \text{BN}(x) = \gamma \left( \frac{x - \mu_B}{\sqrt{\sigma_B^2 + \varepsilon}} \right) + \beta $$

where:

  • μB = Batch Mean
  • σ²B = Batch Variance
  • ε = Small constant for numerical stability

During inference (testing), Batch Normalization uses the running mean and running variance collected during training instead of the current batch statistics.

Benefits of Batch Normalization¶

  • Faster convergence during training.
  • More stable gradients.
  • Less sensitive to learning rate.
  • Reduces internal covariate shift.
  • Provides a small regularization effect, which can improve generalization.

6.3 Train and Compare: With vs Without Batch Normalization¶

In [45]:
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, f1_score

# Baseline Model Prediction
y_pred_base = (model_base.predict(X_test).flatten() > 0.5).astype(int);

# BatchNorm Model Prediction
y_pred_bn = (model_bn.predict(X_test).flatten() > 0.5).astype(int);

print("Baseline ANN")
print("Accuracy :", round(accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred_base),4))
print("F1 Score :", round(f1_score(y_test, y_pred_base),4))

print("\nBatchNorm ANN")
print("Accuracy :", round(accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred_bn),4))
print("F1 Score :", round(f1_score(y_test, y_pred_bn),4))

6.5 Inspect Learned Gamma and Beta¶

In [50]:
# First BatchNorm Layer
bn_layer = model_bn.layers[1]

gamma, beta, moving_mean, moving_variance = bn_layer.get_weights()

print("Gamma Shape:", gamma.shape)
print("Beta Shape :", beta.shape)

Gamma Shape: (128,)
Beta Shape : (128,)
In [51]:
# Gamma Plot
plt.figure(figsize=(12,4))

plt.bar(range(len(gamma)), gamma)

plt.title("Gamma Values")
plt.xlabel("Neuron")
plt.ylabel("Gamma")

plt.show()
In [52]:
# Beta Plot
plt.figure(figsize=(12,4))

plt.bar(range(len(beta)), beta)

plt.title("Beta Values")
plt.xlabel("Neuron")
plt.ylabel("Beta")

plt.show()
  • The Gamma (γ) values show how much each feature is scaled after normalization.
  • The Beta (β) values show the learned shift applied after normalization.
  • Neurons with Gamma values close to zero contribute less to the final prediction.
  • Neurons with larger Gamma values have a stronger influence on the model's output and represent more important learned features.

7.2 Optimiser Convergence Plot¶

In [58]:
histories = {
    "SGD": history_sgd,
    "SGD + Momentum": history_momentum,
    "RMSprop": history_rmsprop,
    "Adam": history_adam,
    "Adam (Explicit)": history_adam_explicit
}

colors = ["blue", "green", "red", "purple", "orange"]
styles = ["-", "--", "-.", ":", "-"]

plt.figure(figsize=(10,6))

for (name, history), color, style in zip(histories.items(), colors, styles):

    val_acc = history.history["val_accuracy"]

    plt.plot(
        val_acc,
        label=name,
        color=color,
        linestyle=style,
        linewidth=2
    )

    # Mark first epoch crossing 83%
    for epoch, acc in enumerate(val_acc):
        if acc >= 0.83:
            plt.axvline(
                x=epoch,
                color=color,
                linestyle=":",
                alpha=0.6
            )
            break

# Reference Lines
plt.axhline(0.80, color="gray", linestyle="--", label="80%")
plt.axhline(0.86, color="black", linestyle="--", label="86%")

plt.title("Optimizer Comparison — Validation Accuracy over 50 Epochs")
plt.xlabel("Epoch")
plt.ylabel("Validation Accuracy")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)

plt.show()
  • The validation accuracy of all five optimizers was compared over 50 epochs.
  • Vertical lines indicate the first epoch where each optimizer reached 83% validation accuracy.
  • The dashed horizontal lines represent the 80% and 86% reference accuracy levels.
  • Adam and RMSprop generally converge faster than SGD, while SGD with Momentum usually performs better than vanilla SGD.

7.3 Why Adam Dominates¶

Why Adam Usually Performs Best¶

1. Vanilla SGD (Stochastic Gradient Descent)¶

  • Uses a fixed learning rate for all parameters.
  • Updates weights using only the current gradient.
  • Does not adapt the learning rate for different features.
  • Converges slowly on high-dimensional datasets such as the Adult Income dataset with one-hot encoded features.

2. SGD with Momentum¶

  • Adds a velocity term that remembers previous updates.
  • Update rule:

$$ v=\beta v-\eta\nabla L $$

  • Momentum smooths oscillations and accelerates movement toward the optimum.
  • Still uses the same learning rate for every parameter.

3. RMSprop¶

  • Maintains a running average of squared gradients.

  • Automatically adjusts the learning rate for each parameter.

  • Works well when gradients change frequently.

  • Usually converges faster than SGD.

4. Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation)¶

Adam combines:

  • Momentum (First Moment) → remembers the direction of previous gradients.
  • RMSprop (Second Moment) → adapts the learning rate for every parameter.

Adam also applies bias correction during the initial training steps:

$$ \theta=\theta-\eta\frac{\hat{m}}{\sqrt{\hat{v}}+\epsilon} $$

where:

  • m = First Moment (Momentum)
  • v = Second Moment (Variance)

This makes Adam stable, fast, and efficient even during the early epochs.

5. Adam (Explicit Parameters)¶

The explicit Adam optimizer confirms the default parameters used in Keras:

  • Learning Rate = 0.001
  • β₁ = 0.9
  • β₂ = 0.999

These values match the original Adam paper by Kingma & Ba (2015).

Conclusion¶

  • Vanilla SGD converges the slowest.
  • SGD with Momentum improves convergence compared to SGD.
  • RMSprop adapts learning rates and usually converges faster.
  • Adam combines Momentum and RMSprop, making it one of the fastest and most stable optimizers for deep learning.
  • On the Adult Income dataset, Adam generally achieves the highest validation accuracy and F1-score while converging in fewer epochs.

Replace the last sentence with your actual experimental result.
Example:

  • Highest Final F1-score: Adam (0.87)
  • Fastest Convergence: Adam (Reached 83% validation accuracy in Epoch 8)

from tensorflow.keras.optimizers import SGD

learning_rates_sgd = [0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1]
history_sgd_lr = {}

for lr in learning_rates_sgd:
    model = build_ann(
        input_dim=X_train.shape[1],
        activation="relu",
        initializer="he_normal",
        use_batch_norm=True,
        optimizer=SGD(learning_rate=lr),
        loss="binary_crossentropy"
    )

    history = model.fit(
        X_train,
        y_train,
        epochs=30,
        batch_size=64,
        validation_split=0.1,
        verbose=0
    )

    history_sgd_lr[lr] = history

    plt.plot(

plt.ylabel("Validation Loss")

plt.grid(True)

for lr, history in history_adam_lr.items():
    plt.plot(
        history.history["val_loss"],
        label=f"lr={lr}"
    )

plt.title("Adam Learning Rate Sensitivity")
plt.xlabel("Epoch")
plt.ylabel("Validation Loss")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)

plt.suptitle("Learning Rate Sensitivity — SGD vs Adam")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Learning Rate Sensitivity: SGD vs Adam¶

Different learning rates were tested for both SGD and Adam optimizers.

SGD¶

  • Very small learning rates (0.0001) result in slow convergence.
  • A moderate learning rate (0.01) usually gives the best performance.
  • A high learning rate (0.1) may cause unstable training or divergence.

Adam¶

  • Adam automatically adapts the learning rate for each parameter.
  • It performs well across a wider range of learning rates.
  • Even when the global learning rate is not optimal, Adam usually converges faster and more stably than SGD.

Therefore, Adam is less sensitive to learning rate selection, while SGD requires careful tuning.

Final ANN Configuration¶

The final model combines the best techniques identified during the experiments:

  • Hidden Layers: 128 → 64
  • Activation Function: ReLU
  • Weight Initialization: He Normal
  • Batch Normalization: Enabled
  • Optimizer: Adam
  • Loss Function: Binary Cross-Entropy (or Weighted BCE if it produced a higher F1-score)
  • Epochs: 80
  • Batch Size: 64

This configuration provides fast convergence, stable training, and strong performance on the Adult Income dataset.

The final model is evaluated using:

  • Accuracy
  • Precision
  • Recall
  • F1-Score
  • ROC-AUC

These metrics provide a complete assessment of the model's classification performance.

from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score, roc_auc_score

# Seven models tracked across the project, evaluated on the held-out test set
model_registry = [
    ("Baseline",         model_base,       "ReLU", "Glorot Uniform", "BCE",          "No",  "Adam"),
    ("Best Activation",  model_elu,        "ELU",  "Glorot Uniform", "BCE",          "No",  "Adam"),
    ("Best Initializer", model_he_normal,  "ReLU", "He Normal",      "BCE",          "No",  "Adam"),
    ("Weighted BCE",     model_wbce,       "ReLU", "He Normal",      "Weighted BCE", "No",  "Adam"),
    ("Focal Loss",       model_focal,      "ReLU", "He Normal",      "Focal Loss",   "No",  "Adam"),
    ("BatchNorm",        model_bn,         "ReLU", "He Normal",      "BCE",          "Yes", "Adam"),
    ("Final Combined",   final_model,      "ReLU", "He Normal",      "Weighted BCE", "Yes", "Adam"),
]

rows = []
for name, mdl, activation, initializer, loss_name, bn_flag, opt_name in model_registry:
    y_prob = mdl.predict(X_test, verbose=0).flatten()
    y_pred = (y_prob > 0.5).astype(int)
    rows.append({
        "Model": name,
        "Activation": activation,
        "Initializer": initializer,
        "Loss": loss_name,
        "BatchNorm": bn_flag,
        "Optimizer": opt_name,
        "Test Accuracy": accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred),
        "Precision": precision_score(y_test, y_pred),
        "Recall": recall_score(y_test, y_pred),
        "F1(1)": f1_score(y_test, y_pred),
        "ROC-AUC": roc_auc_score(y_test, y_prob),
    })

results = pd.DataFrame(rows)
results

from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve, roc_auc_score

models = {
    "Baseline": model_base,
    "Weighted BCE": model_wbce,
    "Final Combined": final_model
}

plt.figure(figsize=(8,6))

for name, model in models.items():

    y_prob = model.predict(X_test).flatten()

    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_test, y_prob)

    auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, y_prob)

    plt.plot(
        fpr,
        tpr,
        linewidth=2,
        label=f"{name} (AUC={auc:.3f})"
    )

plt.plot([0,1],[0,1],"k--")

plt.xlabel("False Positive Rate")
plt.ylabel("True Positive Rate")
plt.title("ROC Curve Comparison")
plt.legend()

plt.grid(True)
plt.show()
